object_types.name: Incident
object_types.definition: A declared or triage-stage occurrence of something breaking, tracked from origin through resolution.

source_references.excerpt: Incident number. INC-, then a sequence.

object_types.name: IncidentNumber
object_types.definition: The unique identifier of an incident, formatted INC- plus a sequence.

source_references.excerpt: Incident number. INC-, then a sequence. ... Unique. And we never delete incidents

object_types.name: Alert
object_types.definition: A notification from the monitoring platform (or a manual alert raised by an engineer) that something may be wrong.

source_references.excerpt: Alert ID. Comes from the monitoring platform.

object_types.name: AlertId
object_types.definition: The unique identifier of an alert, from the monitoring platform.

source_references.excerpt: Alert ID. Comes from the monitoring platform.

object_types.name: Ticket
object_types.definition: A customer support ticket that may originate an incident.

source_references.excerpt: And a ticket has a ticket number. Different system, different format, always has.

object_types.name: TicketNumber
object_types.definition: The unique identifier of a support ticket.

source_references.excerpt: And a ticket has a ticket number.

object_types.name: Severity
object_types.definition: Technical blast-radius classification of an incident, SEV1 (everything down for everyone) through SEV4 (degraded/cosmetic, one region).

source_references.excerpt: SEV1 through SEV4. It's about blast radius and technical impact.

object_types.name: Priority
object_types.definition: Customer-urgency classification of an incident, P1 through P4, based on who's affected, commitments, and SLA breach risk.

source_references.excerpt: And priority is P1 through P4. ... Priority is about customer urgency.

object_types.name: IncidentState
object_types.definition: The current lifecycle state of an incident.

source_references.excerpt: Triage, declared, mitigated, resolved, closed.

object_types.name: Person
object_types.definition: An individual who can serve as incident commander for the duration of an incident.

source_references.excerpt: The incident commander. One person, named, and it's a role for the duration, not a job title.

object_types.name: Team
object_types.definition: A group that owns a service on a standing basis.

source_references.excerpt: A team. Services are owned by teams. People move.

object_types.name: Service
object_types.definition: A system or capability that can be affected by an incident and is owned by exactly one team.

source_references.excerpt: Service name. They're unique, we enforce it in the catalogue.

object_types.name: ServiceName
object_types.definition: The unique name identifying a service.

ambiguities.description: Person (incident commander) identification is assumed to be by name, but the transcript never explicitly states how a person/commander is identified (e.g., employee ID vs. name). Using 'named' loosely as reference mode may not be robust if names are not unique.

source_references.excerpt: The incident commander. One person, named, and it's a role for the duration, not a job title.

ambiguities.description: Team identification is inferred from context (team name) but never explicitly discussed as an identifier in the transcript; confirm whether team name is guaranteed unique.

source_references.excerpt: A team. Services are owned by teams. People move.

ambiguities.description: The 'duplicate' chain rule is stated as intended but explicitly NOT enforced by the system today ('It's not enforced'). It is unclear whether the model should encode the strict asymmetric/acyclic ring constraint as a hard rule or merely document it as an aspirational rule, since real data may currently violate it (two-deep chains have been observed).

source_references.excerpt: It shouldn't. The intent is that everything points at the primary directly. But nothing stops you making a chain and I've seen two-deep ones. ... That's the rule as intended. It's not enforced.

ambiguities.description: Severity and Priority mandatory constraints appear to apply only once an incident is 'declared', not during 'triage'. The current model attaches a general mandatory constraint on Incident, but this is technically only true for declared incidents (mirroring the commander pattern). This mandatory/optionality distinction by state was explicit for commander but was not fully re-examined for severity/priority; clarify whether triage incidents can lack severity/priority values too.

source_references.excerpt: Every declared incident has a severity. That's mandatory, you can't declare without one.
Priority too. Support sets it, and it's on every incident.

ambiguities.description: Whether severity/priority history should be modeled: the transcript notes severity changes over time and is tracked 'in the timeline, as events' but the incident record only carries the current value. It's unclear if the timeline/events concept should be part of this model or is out of scope, and whether priority also changes over time in the same way.

source_references.excerpt: Severity gets revised as we understand the blast radius. That's normal and expected. ... In the timeline, as events. The incident record carries the current severity.

ambiguities.description: Whether an Incident can affect the same Service more than once (e.g., re-affecting after resolution) is unaddressed; internal uniqueness on Incident+Service pair assumed but not explicitly confirmed.

source_references.excerpt: And an incident affects a service? ... One or more. Usually one, sometimes several when it's an infrastructure thing.

ambiguities.description: The classification of customer-caused/user-error incidents for reliability metrics purposes is explicitly parked as an undecided business decision (owned by Ravi) and is NOT modeled. Confirm this remains out of scope until decided.

source_references.excerpt: Whether an incident later found to be caused by customer misconfiguration should be reclassified, excluded from reliability metrics, or left as-is, is undecided. The model today captures the five states and does not include any concept of a cause classification, because there isn't one to capture.

ambiguities.description: The term 'owner' is explicitly flagged by stakeholders as ambiguous/overloaded in everyday conversation, referring to either the Incident Commander or the Service Owner (Team). The model disambiguates this via separate fact types (Incident is commanded by Person vs. Service is owned by Team), but this overload should be flagged for downstream consumers of the model/reports.

source_references.excerpt: Now -- the other 'owner.' ... And in a channel, 'who owns this?' means either. It's genuinely ambiguous every single time.

ambiguities.description: 'Monitoring' as an informal state between mitigated and resolved is explicitly used by people in practice but is not in the system's dropdown. It was excluded from the model per facilitator's decision, but this represents a known gap between informal process and the system of record.

source_references.excerpt: There's also 'monitoring,' which sits between mitigated and resolved. ... If it's not in the system I'm not modelling it. Five states.

ambiguities.description: A 'manual alert' created when an engineer raises something they've spotted is described as 'still an alert' but it's unclear if it should be modeled as a distinct sub-type of Alert (e.g., with a different identification/source) versus the monitoring-platform-generated Alert, since the AlertId is said to come from the monitoring platform specifically.

source_references.excerpt: If an engineer spots something, they raise it, and raising it creates an alert record. It's a manual alert but it's still an alert.
